units.text: Symphony and Beethoven Taxonomy Spec
1. Purpose and scope

This spec says what kind of software Symphony and Beethoven are, what they sit beside, what they add, and what is still unproven. It is the reference the manual's deep research starts from, and the research corrects it.
It places three things:
Symphony, the coordination layer: a claim protocol, a board and workers for Claude Code agents, kept in a GitHub repository and run on GitHub Actions.
Beethoven, the research layer: protocols for grid jobs on Wayne State's cluster, reproducible CLAIM and REFORMS workflows, and checks on code that agents wrote.
The stack they make together, in which Claude iterates the scientific method inside strict frameworks while Symphony coordinates the agents.

Out of scope: the price of the paid SymphonyBoard App, legal opinions on terms of service (raised as open questions only), and the AIDaS grant text, which takes nothing from the coordination experiment until you say so.
Every claim carries one grade:

units.subsection: Symphony: one repository as the shared plane for many agents
units.text: Symphony: one repository as the shared plane for many agents

units.subsection: Symphony: one repository as the shared plane for many agents
units.text: Symphony makes one GitHub repository the shared state for any number of Claude Code workers: a person's local or cloud sessions, routines, and agents running as GitHub Actions jobs. It has no server of its own. The rules are a Python library with no dependencies (symphony-protocol, public, MIT), vendored into each repository beside eleven workflow files and Claude Code hooks in a whole-template copy, or beside at most three workflow files (board, tidy and metrics) and the symphony plugin's hooks in a protocol-only adoption. Verified: PROTOCOL.md, research note 01.

units.subsection: Symphony: one repository as the shared plane for many agents
units.text: Claude runs in only three workflows (claude.yml, the work job of workers.yml and four jobs of coordinator.yml), all through anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 on one subscription token, CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Everything else is deterministic code on the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN, so a worker with nothing to do starts no Claude session. The design rests on about 30 GitHub primitives, among them concurrency queues, branch renames that close a pull request, and environments with required reviewers. Verified: research note 01.

units.subsection: Symphony: one repository as the shared plane for many agents
units.text: Maturity. The library's first commit is 2026-10-10 and release 0.4.1 is of 2026-10-13. Its 1,379 tests and the template's 581 passed on 2026-10-15. A validation harness drives the shipped library through every interleaving of scripted workers against an oracle written from the spec's text: 16.7 million states at depth 8, and 18.8 million with two issues at depth 7, with no violation in the run of 2026-10-14, which searched the library before the fixes of F2, F15, F17, F18 and F19; 93 mutants prove the checks bite. Building the harness and reviewing the fixes it led to found 19 defects: six are fixed in release 0.4.1, eleven more on main ahead of the next release, one (F16) was settled by changing the spec, and one (F8, idleness read from the committer date) waits on the owner (validation/DESIGN.md and known.json). Not built yet: the qa check, the cap of 10 Claude runs a day, the public runtime, the control panel, the account pool, and a benchmark run of Symphony at full scale. Verified: validation run of record, research notes 01 and 12.

units.text: In the owner's words, beethoven-base and beethoven-sites hold the protocols for grid jobs on Wayne State's cluster, beethoven-research the reproducible CLAIM and REFORMS workflows, and beethoven-qa the checks on code that agents write autonomously, while beethoven-agents and symphony-protocol coordinate the agents; Claude iterates the scientific method inside these frameworks. All of Beethoven is private and proprietary. The repositories' roles and their private, proprietary status are Verified (research notes 04 and 05). That symphony-protocol coordinates Beethoven's agents is the owner's design and is in no Beethoven file yet (Inferred; see the next subsection).

units.subsection: How they compose into one stack
units.text: Read from the bottom: the substrate is rented or owned by someone else, sessions run where the work is, Symphony decides who holds which piece of work, tools decide whether the work is acceptable, and the study's checklists decide whether the result may be reported.

units.subsection: How they compose into one stack
units.text: The stack is the owner's design, and its composition is Inferred: no Beethoven repository references Symphony today, and Symphony's own plan rules that no Beethoven repository runs Symphony's code or holds a Claude token. The parts that can be shared are Symphony's Claude-free core (the branch-name claim, the board, the protocol check, the push guard, required checks and auto-merge), because Beethoven forbids a stored Claude token in CI and Symphony's Actions workers need one. Verified: research note 05.
3. The taxonomy

No published taxonomy answers the question this spec asks. The academic taxonomies of agents read for it (2024 to 2026) classify by architecture, control structure, interaction type, autonomy, environment, memory and domain; none has an axis for where the compute runs and who pays for it (Inferred from the dozen read, not a systematic review; research note 13). Industry categories moved in 2025 and 2026 from assistants to agents: Gartner's 2025 report was a Magic Quadrant for AI Code Assistants (Reported, from a news digest), and a single secondary page, possibly machine-written, reports a 2026 Magic Quadrant for Enterprise AI Coding Agents (Reported). Thoughtworks' Technology Radar Vol 34 (April 2026) named "agent-native project memory and task tracking" a new category, with Beads as its example, put a small team of coding agents in Assess and coding agent swarms in Caution (Reported, from a dataset of the radar). The CNCF landscape has an AI Agent category with eleven subcategories, none for coding agents or for coordinating them (Verified, landscape.yml).
The taxonomy below keeps the axes that recur in that literature and adds the one it lacks. An axis earns its place only if it separates the neighbors in section 5.

Three axes carry this study. Axis 10 is where the Actions story lives and the one no taxonomy has. Axis 5 is where Symphony's claim sits: a claim made by creating a branch, a lease-like release and optimistic merging. Axis 11 is where Beethoven's claim sits: a tool, never a model, decides. Axes 1, 3 and 7 locate the neighbors.

The classical frames fit closely. Malone and Crowston define coordination as "managing dependencies among activities" and name four families of dependency, one of which, producer and consumer, splits into prerequisite, transfer and usability (Reported, from mirrors of the paper; research note 13). Each of the six kinds has a counterpart in agent work: claiming an issue is a shared resource, a blocker is a prerequisite, a pull request is a transfer, a required check is a usability standard, the landing order of overlapping work is simultaneity, and an epic is task and subtask (Inferred; research note 13).
4. Placement

Two of the twelve axes separate Symphony from its neighbors at a glance: where the coordination state lives, and what one more agent run costs as each system is usually run. Positions inside a quadrant mean nothing; only the quadrant is a claim, and each is sourced in section 5.
[EMBED node/3dde4a85-438e: Coordinators by where their state lives and what one more run costs · zones only, not measured positions]

The tinted corner, a flat price with the state on the forge, holds five systems. unsorry, a Lean proof swarm, claims by pushing claim files to one shared branch, expires them with a two-hour timer in Actions and renders its board in Actions, but its agents run on volunteers' machines. agentic-setup claims by creating a branch, but its orchestrator is a local session. CCPM claims by setting an assignee and a label, which two agents can both do. aeon runs one agent's scheduled skills in Actions with no claims between workers. Symphony is the only one there that puts agents running in Actions and people's own sessions under one claim rule (Inferred from research/taxonomy/verify/03, whose rows show none of the other four with such a rule; section 8). Below the line, the gh-aw work queue is Symphony's closest neighbor: it too makes a claim atomic with a compare-and-swap on a git ref, but a trusted scheduler grants claims only to Actions runs, a claim ends when its run ends rather than after idle time, and it sits there because its Claude engine takes an API key, workload identity or Copilot credits and refuses the subscription token (Verified, research/taxonomy/verify/01).

6. Integration
6.1 What the stack depends on

Symphony: GitHub (issues, labels, refs, Actions, rulesets, environments, a GitHub App for the first commit and the sync), anthropics/claude-code-action@v1, Claude Code's hooks, and Python 3.12's standard library. Nothing else: the writing rules forbid new dependencies.

Beethoven: Slurm, Apptainer and Open OnDemand at the university, Claude Code's Remote Control, Chrome for the extension, and icontract, CrossHair and Z3 for the gate; Metaflow with metaflow-slurm is chosen but not built, and metaflow-slurm is a 0.0.4 release from 2024 that drives sbatch over SSH with a key file, which conflicts with Beethoven's rule never to touch a credential unless its planned plain sbatch adapter replaces it (Verified, research note 11).

6.3 What it composes with

GitHub's own gates fold into Symphony's planned qa check: CodeQL, dependency review and secret scanning, free on a public repository (Verified for CodeQL and secret scanning; GitHub's own pages disagree on dependency review, as section 9.2 says; the qa check is not built).
beethoven-qa is planned as the Python design-by-contract lane of that qa check (a recorded decision; not built).

Other coding agents could claim under the same rule if they push claude/N with a claim file: the protocol is agent-neutral in shape, but Copilot's cloud agent and gh-aw name their own branches, so each would need an adapter (Inferred; Open).
gh-aw could run as a kind of Symphony worker, its safe outputs opening the pull request, or Symphony's board could read gh-aw's queue; neither exists (Inferred; depends on section 5's comparison).
GitHub's merge queue can land work after Symphony orders overlapping pieces; the two are complementary (Inferred).

Workflow managers for Beethoven's outer loop: Snakemake (with a Slurm executor plugin), Nextflow, Parsl or CWL are alternatives to the chosen Metaflow; DVC for data versions; MLflow or Weights and Biases for run records (Verified as products, research note 11).
The Symphony plugin in symphony-marketplace brings the skills, /board and the hooks to a repository not made from the template.
6.4 What it could replace
A coordination server of the project's own (a paperclip server, a Beads Dolt server, an openai/symphony daemon) for a team whose work already lives on GitHub (Inferred).
Convention-only claiming, such as CCPM's assignee and label, which two agents can set at once (Inferred, research note 07).
For Beethoven, the checklist tables authors fill after the fact, if the gates are built and shown to catch what reviewers miss (Open, question R8).

units.subsection: 6.5 Where Symphony and Beethoven meet today
units.text: 6.5 Where Symphony and Beethoven meet today

units.subsection: 6.5 Where Symphony and Beethoven meet today
units.text: Nowhere in code. Symphony's plan says no Beethoven repository runs Symphony's code or holds a Claude token; a Markdown-only pilot of the claim protocol in beethoven-qa is an open owner question, recommended yes after Symphony's Phase 3 (Verified, research note 05). The grant packet puts its agent under the laboratory's claim protocol of one issue, one branch, one pull request, and names neither Symphony nor symphony-protocol (Verified, research note 05). That protocol matches Symphony's rule without its Actions workers (Inferred: spine-program, the repository the packet builds on, adopted Symphony's protocol alone on 2026-10-12, according to the template's checkpoints).
7. The need
Three problems, each with its evidence. The strength of each source is stated, because the evidence is uneven.

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: The curse of coordination. CooperBench (Stanford and SAP Labs, preprint, 2026) gave 652 feature pairs from 12 repositories either to one agent or to two agents in isolated workspaces that could only message each other. One agent passed far more often: GPT-5 315 against 183 of 652 (48.3% against 28.1%), Claude Sonnet 4.5 307 against 168 (47.1% against 25.8%). The paper states the gap three ways (30% in the abstract, up to 50% in section 4, 41% in appendix C), so quote the counts. Verified, the paper's PDF in the cooperbench/website repository.

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: What fails is duplicated or incompatible work, not skill. Of the failed two-agent runs, 33.2% were work overlap and 29.7% divergent architecture; in 50 hand-read traces the root causes were expectation (42%), commitment (32%) and communication (26%). Messaging took up to 20% of the agents' steps and did not raise success. A plan in the first turn nearly halved the conflict rate (29.4% against 51.5%). Verified, same paper.

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: Git alone is not enough; a shared substrate with a task list is. Giving each pair a git server moved success by only 1 to 3 points (Verified, the February 2026 post in the cooperbench/website repository). In CooperBench's later ablation (50 pairs, one seed, one model) messaging alone reached 26%, one agent 48%, a shared git remote 56%, and a lead with a shared task list and scratchpad 62%; removing the task list or the scratchpad dropped the team below one agent. Weak evidence (n = 50, one seed), but it points the same way. Verified, the CooperBench repository at 63b9d44.

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: The field shows the same. Merge-simulating 107,026 agent pull requests found textual conflicts in 27.67% (AgenticFlict, Verified), and 40.2% of popular repositories in the AIDev dataset had agent pull requests open at the same time (Reported).

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: Practitioners converge on claims, ownership and gates. Anthropic's 16-agent C compiler claimed tasks by writing lock files that git refused a second agent (Verified); Claude Code agent teams claim tasks under a file lock and advise each teammate to own different files (Verified); Cursor reports that naive locks collapsed 20 agents to the throughput of two or three, because locks were held too long or never released (Reported).

units.subsection: 7.1 Agents that share a codebase collide, and chat does not fix it
units.text: The owner's own replication (coordbench) has run 8 pairs: Symphony's arm passed 6 of 8 like every two-agent arm, one agent 5 of 8, and no difference is significant (every exact McNemar p is 1.000; Verified, research note 03). It is a pilot, and its token and dollar figures are inflated by a prompt of about 78,000 to 82,000 tokens that every agent there inherits (Verified, research note 03). It stays out of the grant until you say so.

Section 11 makes this the first research question.

units.subsection: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it
units.text: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it

units.subsection: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it
units.text: Luo, Kasirzadeh and Shah (NeurIPS 2025) found data leakage, inappropriate benchmarks, metric misuse and post-hoc selection in two AI-scientist systems, and found them far easier to detect from trace logs and code than from the paper (Reported).

units.subsection: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it
units.text: Beel and colleagues found 5 of 12 proposed experiments (42%) failed on coding errors, with some hallucinated numbers (Reported; n = 12). Kosmos reports 79.4% of its statements judged accurate, so about one in five is not (Reported).

units.subsection: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it
units.text: Reporting checklists are filled by authors after the fact: a 2025 umbrella review put median CLAIM compliance at 68% across 421 studies, and in 2024 only 5 of 98 imaging journals encouraged AI-specific reporting guidelines (Reported). No AI-scientist system found enforces REFORMS, CLAIM, TRIPOD+AI or a similar checklist as a gate (Inferred; an absence claim from a search that ran out of budget).

units.subsection: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it
units.text: Code written by agents is often insecure: on SusVibes (ICML 2026), Claude Opus 4.8 in Claude Code passes 83.9% of tasks functionally but only 32.8% both functionally and securely (Verified from the leaderboard's submission files; the entries are self-submitted).

units.subsection: 7.2 Agent-driven research fails where the paper cannot show it
units.text: This is the gap Beethoven's design names: gates that read the agent's run record, not its paper, and fail the run when a checklist item is unmet. It is almost entirely unbuilt (section 2).

units.subsection: 7.3 Cost and setup keep coordination out of reach
units.text: 7.3 Cost and setup keep coordination out of reach

units.subsection: 7.3 Cost and setup keep coordination out of reach
units.text: Coordination multiplies tokens: Anthropic measured multi-agent research systems at about 15 times the tokens of chat, and Claude Code's agent teams at about 7 times a standard session in plan mode (Verified, research system, costs). The 16-agent C compiler cost just under $20,000 in API fees over two weeks (Verified).

units.subsection: 7.3 Cost and setup keep coordination out of reach
units.text: The neighbors that run agents in CI meter every run: gh-aw's Claude engine takes an API key or Copilot credits, openai/codex-action needs an API key, and Copilot's agents spend AI credits at $0.01 each as well as Actions minutes (Verified, research note 10), though GitHub's docs do not say whether the cloud agent's minutes are free on a public repository (research/taxonomy/verify/01).

units.subsection: 7.3 Cost and setup keep coordination out of reach
units.text: Free CI for open source has shrunk everywhere but GitHub: Travis CI ended unlimited open-source builds in 2020, GitLab.com put public projects on quotas from 2021, Azure DevOps stopped new public projects in 2026 and will make the existing ones private in 2027, pointing them to GitHub, and Cirrus CI stopped running jobs on 2026-06-01 (Verified from their docs for GitLab's quotas today and for Azure; Reported for GitLab's 2021 start and the rest). Section 9 takes this up.
8. What is unique

Every single mechanism Symphony uses has prior art. What may be unique is the combination, and three of its parts. Each claim below names the observation that would refute it. Symphony's three claims, U1 to U3, were put to an adversarial search of 25 candidates on 2026-10-15 (research/taxonomy/verify/03); none had four of the five mechanisms below, but one, unsorry, has (c) and looser forms of (a), (b) and (d), so the claims are worded narrowly. Beethoven's three, U4 to U6, were not part of that search; they rest on narrower searches in research notes 04, 11 and 12.

The five mechanisms: (a) a claim made atomic by a git ref on the shared forge; (b) automatic release of an idle claim by a CI job, keeping the work; (c) a board and coordinator that run as CI jobs with state only in forge objects; (d) people's own sessions and agents in CI under one claim rule, on a flat-rate subscription; (e) validation of the shipped protocol code by exhaustive interleavings against an oracle written from the spec, with mutants.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: 9.1 What "Actions-native" means here

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: Symphony's coordinator is not a service that talks to GitHub; it is a set of GitHub Actions jobs that run when GitHub says something happened. The board, the idle-claim release, the overlap notices, the dealing of work to workers, the protocol check and the cleanup are deterministic code on the workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN, with no Claude call and no server. GitHub's own events trigger them, GitHub's concurrency queue serializes them, GitHub's refs make the claim atomic, and GitHub's rulesets and required checks enforce the result. Claude runs only where judgment is needed, as a job on the same runners. Verified, research note 01.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: 9.2 What is free

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: GitHub's docs: "Use of the standard GitHub-hosted runners is free and unlimited on public repositories" (supported-github-runners.md, Verified 2026-10-15). Self-hosted runners are free on every plan.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: A public repository gets twice the machine a private one does: Linux and Windows standard runners with 4 vCPUs, 16 GB and a 14 GB SSD, against 2 vCPUs and 8 GB in a private repository. Verified.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: The governance a coordination protocol needs is free there too: rulesets, required checks and code owners on GitHub Free, environments with required reviewers and wait timers (which on Free, Pro and Team exist only for public repositories), CodeQL code scanning, secret scanning with push protection, and Dependabot. Symphony's gate and its owner-approved release environment rely on this. Verified; GitHub's own pages disagree on whether dependency review is free on a public repository, and most say it is.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: GitHub announced a $0.002-a-minute charge on self-hosted runners on 2025-12-16 and withdrew it from the docs the next day; secondary sources say it is postponed, not cancelled (Verified from the github/docs history; Reported for the postponement).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: 9.4 What still costs money

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: Inference is never free. Symphony's Actions workers run on one person's Claude plan through CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (Pro $20 a month, or $17 billed annually; Max $100 or $200), and they share that plan's five-hour window and weekly limit with the person's own use. The Max and Team monthly API credits do not cover runs of the Claude Code GitHub Action. Verified, research note 10.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: A private repository gets 2,000 included minutes a month on Free, 3,000 on Pro and Team, 50,000 on Enterprise Cloud, then $0.006 a minute on Linux (since 2026-01-01), each job rounded up to a whole minute, and usage stops at the quota without a payment method. Rulesets that enforce the gate need Pro or Team there. Verified.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: An illustration (Inferred; the workload is an assumption): ten one-hour Claude runs a day is 18,000 runner minutes a month. On a public repository that costs nothing in minutes. On a private repository on Team it is 15,000 minutes over the quota, about $90 a month, before the board's own runs, each of which bills at least a minute.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: AI review layers (Copilot code review, GitHub's AI Scan, Claude Code Review) bill credits even on public repositories; Symphony's rules keep them out of the gate. Verified, research note 12.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: 9.5 The terms that govern it

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: GitHub's Actions terms (effective 2026-04-27) forbid offering Actions "or any elements of the Actions product or service, for commercial purposes", disproportionate burden, and, on GitHub-hosted runners, "any other activity unrelated to the production, testing, deployment, or publication of the software project associated with the repository" (Verified, github/site-policy). Agents writing and testing the repository's own code sit inside that line (Inferred). A benchmark that runs other projects' tasks, and a paid App whose runtime rides each customer's free minutes, need a reading (Open, question R5).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: Anthropic documents the subscription token for claude-code-action and says runs then "use your Claude subscription instead of API billing", but advises an API key for a secret shared across repositories, since the token is tied to one person's plan; its legal page says plan limits "assume ordinary, individual usage" (Verified, GitHub Actions, legal and compliance). Whether several Actions workers on one plan are ordinary, individual usage is not stated (Open, question R6).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: Claude Code's docs say bare mode will become the default for claude -p and that bare mode does not read the OAuth token; whether claude-code-action will keep the subscription path working is not stated (Open, question R6).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: 9.6 Why it matters

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: A coordination step costs nothing. Claiming, releasing, ordering overlaps and rendering the board are runner minutes on GITHUB_TOKEN, free on a public repository, with no model call. Neighbors that coordinate with a model, or through a hosted service, pay for every step.

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: A Claude run costs plan usage, not dollars. Until the plan's window is reached, one more worker run has no metered price. Of the neighbors examined that run agents in Actions, gh-aw, openai/codex-action and Copilot's agents meter inference by the token or the credit; aeon runs one agent on the subscription token but coordinates no claims (sections 5 and 8).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: There is nothing to host. No server, database or daemon of the project's own: the forge is the lock, the CI is the scheduler, and the repository is the state. That removes the setup and the bill that keep a coordinator out of a small project, and it survives the churn of agent frameworks (section 5).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: The offer is GitHub's alone, so far. No other major hosted CI found still offers new public projects unlimited free minutes (Azure Pipelines keeps them only for existing public projects, until those turn private in 2027): section 7.3 lists who withdrew, and CircleCI caps open source at 400,000 credits a month (Reported, from its pricing page by search). That is also a dependency: one vendor's pricing decides the economics (section 10).

units.section: 9. GitHub Actions nativeness and free public minutes
units.text: It does not reach Beethoven as built. Beethoven's repositories are private and its science needs the cluster and GPUs, which Actions never gives free. Actions fits Beethoven as the control and verification plane, with the cluster as the compute plane, as its CI already does: the gate runs on GitHub's runners and a grid lane posts commit statuses back. A public Beethoven gate library would run free (Inferred).

The server enforces a claim only at its creation

Git refuses a second creation of claude/N, but GitHub accepts a fast-forward or forced push onto an existing claim under the recommended setup, since rulesets must leave claude/** alone. Only the local push guard refuses forced pushes, and on 2026-10-15 it was found to read the session's own directory rather than the clone a git -C command names, so a lease onto another worker's claim passed when run from a directory whose clone had neither branch, though it was refused from either worker's own clone
research/taxonomy/verify/02; a fix to the guard; question R4
The idle clock is the pusher's

Idleness is read from the head commit's committer date, which the pusher writes: a commit dated in the future holds a claim indefinitely, against the coordinator and a person's release alike, and one dated in the past is released at once. This is finding F8, open in 0.4.1 and on main
The unmerged F8 fix reads GitHub's record of the push, falling back to the commit date when that record is missing; question R4
A reopened issue can be orphaned
The labels claimed and in-review stay on a closed issue; if it is reopened, the board lists it nowhere and no worker is dealt it until a person takes them off
A board rule for reopened issues; question R4

Whether a public, Claude-free Beethoven gate library is wanted, which is the only way Beethoven gets free minutes.
Which subset of the taxonomy's twelve axes a short public explanation should use (the manual proposes three).
Whether the experiment, once complete, belongs in this spec; it stays out of the grant until you say so.
11. Research questions
Each question owns the Open claims named in it. A question is answered only when its acceptance criteria are met; until then the claim keeps its grade.
Question
Answered when
R1
Does Symphony's protocol beat one agent, and the other two-agent arms, at a matched budget?

The coordbench full run you chose on 2026-10-15 (35 new pairs under five arms, plus the runs to redo) reports pass rates with exact tests and confidence intervals, and tokens, wall time and list-price dollars per pair; any gap under the roughly 15-point noise floor is reported as not established
R2
Is the combination in section 8 unique?

A documented search (FSE, ICSE and ASE 2026, arXiv cs.SE and cs.MA, GitHub topics, the awesome lists of agent orchestrators) scores every candidate on the five mechanisms of section 8; claim U1 stands only if none has four of the five, or (a), (c) and (d) together
R3
What does one coordination step cost, and which GitHub limit binds first?

The canary measures API calls per board run, the medians from claim to first pull request and from open to merge, and the number of concurrent workers at which GITHUB_TOKEN's 1,000 requests an hour or the 100-run queue gives out; the library retries on 429 and secondary limits
R4
Does the claim hold on github.com as it does on a local git server?

The canary records a second creation of claude/N, a push that descends from another worker's claim, a forced push with and without a ruleset, the rename on release, and a push after a merge; the clock question of F8 is settled
R5
Are Actions workers, benchmarks and a paid App inside GitHub's Actions terms?

GitHub's written answer, or a lawyer's reading, on three cases: Claude workers writing the repository's own code; coordbench running other projects' tasks; SymphonyBoard's open runtime running in customers' Actions
R6
Can several Actions workers run on one person's subscription token, and will that keep working?

Anthropic's written answer on a token in an organization secret, several parallel workers on one plan as ordinary, individual usage, and claude-code-action under bare mode; and a tested fallback that uses an API key
R7
What are free public minutes worth to an adopter?

For three workloads (one maintainer, a small team, a research lab), the monthly minutes and their price on a private repository, and the same work's price on gh-aw with an API key and on Copilot's agents in credits, with every assumption stated and every price linked
R8
Do Beethoven's checklist gates catch what reviewers miss?

REFORMS and CLAIM gates built for the first study catch seeded faults of the kinds Luo et al. found (leakage, post-hoc selection, metric misuse) that a reading of the paper alone misses; and a search names any other system that gates these checklists in code, or finds none
R9
Does the taxonomy separate the field?

Every system in section 5 is placed on all twelve axes with sources, no two systems practitioners treat as different share all twelve cells, and a systematic search confirms or refutes that no published taxonomy has a compute-payer axis
How much does the name cost?
The first page of results on the main search engines and registries for Symphony with agents, coding or Claude is captured, with a recommendation: keep it, qualify it, or rename
